newsitem.title: ZAIRE: MOBUTU FACES MOUNTING PRESSURE TO RELINQUISH POWER.
newsitem.headline: MOBUTU FACES MOUNTING PRESSURE TO RELINQUISH POWER.

text.p: Rebels dealt a potentially fatal blow to the 32-year rule of President Mobutu Sese Seko by wresting control of Zaire's economic backbone.

With the capital Kinshasa gripped by anti-Mobutu unrest on Wednesday, Laurent Kabila's rebels entered Zaire's southern copper capital Lubumbashi, the biggest prize in their six-month campaign to topple the president.
Kabila's forces took the diamond hub of Mbuji-Mayi last week and now hold about half the territory of Africa's third largest nation, including all the mainstay mineral-producing provinces.
They entered Lubumbashi after stiff resistance from Mobutu loyalists on the approaches to the city of one million people.

"The fall of Lubumbashi is the total collapse of Mobutu because if Mobutu is intelligent he will realise that he must resign and has no other choice,'' Louis Nyarubasa, a rebel spokesman, said at their headquarters in Goma in the east.
After nightfall, witnesses said gunfire could still be heard in Lubumbashi and the army was reported to be in control of the airport six km (four miles) to the north.
The United States added to the pressure on Mobutu by urging an end to "dictatorship'' in Zaire.

"We do know one thing, we think the time for dictatorship is over in Zaire and the time for stability and democracy, if democracy can be achieved -- we think that time is approaching,'' said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said it was time for an "orderly transition'' in Zaire and that "we want everyone to cooperate to make that orderly transition possible''.
"I think that it's clear that we have to move beyond President Mobutu and think about how we can structure a government that will meet the needs of the Zairean people,'' McCurry said.

The United States and other Western allies have stationed about 1,000 troops in Brazzaville, the Congo capital across the River Zaire from Kinshasa, to evacuate their nationals from Zaire in case of a breakdown of law and order.
However, U.S. embassy sources said unrest in Kinshasa had not yet reached the stage where evacuations were necessary.

Mobutu on Wednesday named a senior general as emergency prime minister in a move that seemed a desperate bid to reassert his dwindling authority in the capital, where his army clashed with angry opposition supporters.
"We won't take this lying down. They will find us in their path,'' one Tshisekedi aide said on hearing that Mobutu had appointed General Likulia Bolongo prime minister.
Mobutu, 66, decreed a nationwide state of emergency on Tuesday and sacked newly appointed prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, his arch-foe, on Wednesday.
His army clashed in Kinshasa on Wednesday with thousands of supporters of the veteran opposition leader, who was prime minister for less than a week.
Tshisekedi, his eyes streaming from the effects of tear gas, tried in vain to make his way to the prime minister's office complex on foot to install his new team.
Likulia was defence minister in the pre-Tshisekedi administration of Kengo wa Dondo. Parliament voted out Kengo after persistent charges that he mismanaged the war.
Likulia said his government would crack down on lawbreakers and attempt to restore order to the crumbling state.
"The priority objective is to restore public order and the pacification of our country by removing all the problems leading to the breakup of our nation,'' he told reporters.
He ruled out any thought of Mobutu stepping down, saying it was not for the United States to call for Mobutu's departure.
